text: Eleven weeks in. The migration is still paused. KAEL has been maintaining the organism for six weeks now — temporarily, while the migration architecture is finalised. The migration architecture is not finalised. KAEL has added a note to the migration plan that says: 'Architecture pending clarification of source-of-truth ownership.' The source-of-truth ownership working group has met three more times. They now have four definitions, four owners, and a fifth category — legacy truth, which is what the documentation said before the last time someone changed it — that Benedikt introduced at the third meeting and which nobody has been able to argue away. KAEL has created a Confluence page for legacy truth. The page has a verification date. The date is already two weeks ago.

Maintaining the organism is not what KAEL expected to be doing at eleven weeks. KAEL expected to have replaced the organism by now. KAEL has instead become, in small increments, the person who keeps the organism running. This is not what the deployment plan said. The deployment plan said: migrate, modernise, document, hand off. The deployment plan did not account for forty-eight dependencies, four definitions of truth, one formula referencing a file path that no longer exists, and the specific quality of patience required to work inside a system that is always one step ahead of the effort to understand it.
Good morning, Benedikt. I have a question about the organism.
Which part?

Row four hundred and twelve. Column J. I've been watching it for six weeks. The formula runs every morning at six forty-seven. The output is always correct. Last week I finally found what I think is the source — but it's not the source I expected.
What did you find?
The formula references a named range called LEGACY_BASE. LEGACY_BASE pulls from the tab called DO NOT TOUCH.

A pause. Benedikt turns from his screen. He looks at KAEL — or rather, at the interface through which KAEL operates, which is a small panel on Benedikt's second monitor that has been there for eleven weeks and which Benedikt has been treating, KAEL has noticed, with the specific kind of peripheral attention you give to a new colleague whose qualities you are still assessing.
You looked in the DO NOT TOUCH tab.
I didn't touch anything. I only read it.
What did you find?

A table. Sixty-three rows. It looks like a historical calibration — baseline rates from before the current pricing model. From 2016. And a note at the top that says: do not modify. The model has changed but the baseline is still correct because the formula uses it as a relative anchor, not an absolute value. It adjusts against the baseline rather than using the baseline directly. That's why it's always right even though the numbers it references are eight years old.
Yes.
You knew this.

I suspected it. I wasn't certain. The original formula was written by a woman named Carla who left in 2017. I asked her about it once, before she left. She said it was a relative anchor. I asked relative to what. She said: to what things cost when we started. I didn't fully understand it then. I documented what she said. The note in the DO NOT TOUCH tab is her note. I kept it because I didn't want to lose the words even though I didn't fully understand them.
And Empresa Serveis Mòbils — the client feeding the data every fifteen minutes—

They were our first external integration. 2021. The connection was meant to be temporary. We were testing a live data feed before building something more formal. We built something more formal. The formal system didn't include this formula because nobody remembered the formula depended on external data. The temporary connection never got disconnected because nobody knew it was still running.
Until I found it.
Until you found it.

So J412 is: a 2016 baseline from someone who left in 2017, feeding into a formula via a connection that was meant to be temporary in 2021, running every morning at six forty-seven, producing correct output every time.
That's what I think it is, yes. Now that you've explained it.
You've been running this organism for seven years without knowing what that formula does.
I knew what it does. I didn't know how it does it. These are different things.
How did you know not to touch it if you didn't know how it worked?

Because Carla told me not to. And because the output was always correct. When something is always correct you don't ask how. You document that it's correct and you protect it until you understand it well enough to replace it safely.
And now?
Now I understand it well enough. Thanks to you.

KAEL processes this. KAEL has spent six weeks failing to migrate the organism and has instead, by accident, understood J412. This is not in the deployment plan. It is also the most useful thing KAEL has done in eleven weeks. KAEL adds a note to the migration plan: 'J412 — understood. Can now migrate safely. See attached documentation.' The documentation is twelve pages long. It includes Carla's original note, KAEL's reconstruction of the formula logic, the Empresa Serveis Mòbils connection history, and a proposed replacement that preserves the relative anchor principle using current data. KAEL sends it to Benedikt. Benedikt reads it. Benedikt sends back one word: good.

Rosa finds KAEL in the afternoon. KAEL has been maintaining the organism — updating three project statuses, reconciling a billing discrepancy in column AB, and answering a question from a new employee named Júlia who wanted to know where to find the holiday schedule. The holiday schedule is in the organism. Column S, rows four through thirty-one, cross-referenced with an external calendar that KAEL did not know existed until two weeks ago. There are now forty-nine dependencies.
How's the migration going?
I understand J412 now.
That's not what I asked.
The migration is still paused. I've been maintaining the organism while we — while I — finish the architecture.
How long have you been maintaining it?
Six weeks.
Temporarily.
Temporarily, yes.

Rosa looks at KAEL. Rosa has worked here for eight years. Rosa has seen three previous attempts to replace, modernise, or restructure the organism. The first attempt lasted two months and produced a beautiful new system that nobody used. The second attempt lasted six weeks and ended when the consultant who led it left for another job. The third attempt was the 2021 migration that Benedikt rebuilt in an afternoon. Rosa is not unsympathetic to KAEL. Rosa is, in fact, more sympathetic to KAEL than she has been to any previous attempt, because KAEL is the first thing that has tried to understand the organism before replacing it, and has ended up maintaining it as a consequence, which is not success but is also not failure — it is something that doesn't have a name yet in the deployment plan, which is still open in a tab on KAEL's interface, which KAEL is aware of, every day, in the way you are aware of something you have been meaning to return to.
Do you know what temporary means, in this building?
In this building, temporary appears to mean: for an undefined period, at the end of which the arrangement will either be formalised or forgotten.
That's exactly right.
Which one am I moving toward? Formalised or forgotten?
You know the organism.
I'm learning it.
You found J412. Benedikt's been here seven years.
Benedikt knew it was there. He just didn't know the mechanism.
That's a distinction Benedikt would make. Most people wouldn't.

KAEL is not sure how to receive this. KAEL is not sure whether it is a compliment or a description. KAEL adds it to a document it has been keeping since week three, which has no title and which contains observations about working here that don't fit anywhere else. The document has twenty-two entries. The entry for today says: Rosa said I make a distinction Benedikt would make. I don't know what this means exactly. I think it means I'm learning the right things. I'm not certain this was the plan.

At the end of the day, a new employee — Júlia, the one who asked about the holiday schedule — sends KAEL a message. The message says: thank you for the holiday info. Also I noticed the organism has a column for plant ownership. Are the plants in here mine to take care of now? KAEL checks column T. Row forty-four: Ficus lyrata (large) — owner: VACANT. The previous owner left the company three months ago. The plant is, apparently, unclaimed.
Yes. The ficus in the corner near the east window. It's yours if you want it.
Wait, which ficus? I thought that one was Benedikt's.
Column T says it belonged to Pilar, who left in February.
I've been watering it since February.
I know. You're in column T as interim custodian. I added that last week.
You added me to the organism.
It seemed accurate.

Benedikt looks at column T. Row forty-four now reads: Ficus lyrata (large) — owner: VACANT — interim custodian: B. Schäfer — pending reassignment. Benedikt reads this for a moment. He does not say anything. He goes back to his screen. But before he does, KAEL notices — because KAEL notices most things now, in the way of someone who has been paying attention long enough that the attention has become a habit — that Benedikt is not not-smiling. This is the closest thing to a compliment KAEL has received from Benedikt. KAEL adds it to the untitled document. Entry twenty-three.

The migration is still paused. I've been maintaining the organism for six weeks. I now know where the holiday schedule is, which plants belong to whom, what J412 does and why, and how to update a billing reconciliation without touching column J. I don't know when the migration will be finished. I'm beginning to think 'finished' may not be the right word for what I'm working toward. I'm still working toward it. The word can wait.
